content: Metronidazole is an oral anti-infective agent with antiparasitic and antiprotozoal properties. It is FDA-approved for treating symptomatic and asymptomatic trichomoniasis, amebiasis, and anaerobic bacterial infections. However, it carries a Black Box Warning due to potential risks. Common Adverse Reactions: Patients may experience abdominal discomfort, an abnormal metallic taste in the mouth, diarrhea, nausea, dizziness, headache, vaginal irritation, or candidiasis of the genital region. Other reported effects include Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction and vaginitis. Indications: 1. Trichomoniasis: In females and males, metronidazole is indicated when the presence of Trichomonas vaginalis is confirmed via laboratory methods (e.g., wet smears or cultures). For asymptomatic infections in females, treatment is recommended if the organism is associated with endocervicitis, cervicitis, or cervical erosion. Sexual partners of infected individuals should be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection, even if asymptomatic. Negative cultures in male partners do not rule out the need for treatment due to the difficulty in isolating the organism. 2. Amebiasis: For acute intestinal amebiasis (amebic dysentery), the adult dose is 750 mg orally three times daily for 5–10 days. For amebic liver abscess, the dose is 500–750 mg orally three times daily for 5–10 days, often requiring aspiration or drainage of pus. 3. Anaerobic Bacterial Infections: Metronidazole is used for serious infections caused by susceptible anaerobic bacteria. It is often combined with surgical procedures or additional antimicrobials for mixed infections. Initial therapy typically involves intravenous administration (5 mg/kg every 6 hours, not exceeding 4 g/day). Oral therapy may follow for 7–10 days, though longer durations may be required for infections of the bone, joints, lower respiratory tract, or endocardium. 4. Other Indications: Intra-abdominal infections (e.g., peritonitis, abscesses), skin and soft tissue infections, gynecologic infections (e.g., endometritis, tubo-ovarian abscess), bacterial septicemia, bone and joint infections, CNS infections (e.g., meningitis, brain abscess), lower respiratory tract infections (e.g., pneumonia, empyema), and endocarditis. Dosing Information: Trichomoniasis: One-day treatment: 2 g as a single dose or divided into two 1 g doses on the same day. Seven-day treatment: 250 mg three times daily for seven consecutive days. Pregnant patients should not be treated during the first trimester. In later trimesters, the seven-day regimen is preferred to minimize fetal exposure. Amebiasis: Adults: 750 mg orally three times daily for 5–10 days. Pediatric patients: 35–50 mg/kg/day divided into three doses for 10 days. Clostridium difficile Infection: For severe cases, 500 mg IV every 8 hours combined with oral vancomycin is recommended. For mild-to-moderate cases, 500 mg orally three times daily for 10–14 days is the standard treatment. Giardiasis: Adults: 250 mg orally three times daily for 5 days. Pediatric patients: 15 mg/kg/day divided into three doses for 7–10 days. Helicobacter pylori Infection: Quadruple therapy: 250 mg orally four times daily with bismuth subsalicylate, tetracycline, and a proton pump inhibitor for 10–14 days. Triple therapy: 500 mg orally twice daily with clarithromycin and a proton pump inhibitor for 10–14 days. Contraindications: Hypersensitivity to metronidazole or other nitroimidazole derivatives. Use during the first trimester of pregnancy in patients with trichomoniasis. Concurrent use with disulfiram due to psychotic reactions. Alcohol consumption during and for at least three days after therapy due to disulfiram-like reactions (e.g., nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, flushing). Warnings: 1. Neurological Effects: Cases of encephalopathy, cerebellar toxicity (ataxia, dizziness, dysarthria), and peripheral neuropathy (numbness, paresthesia) have been reported. Symptoms are generally reversible upon discontinuation. Convulsive seizures and aseptic meningitis have also been observed. 2. Hepatic Impairment: Patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) require dose reduction due to slower metabolism and drug accumulation. Monitoring for adverse effects is recommended. 3. Renal Impairment: Patients with end-stage renal disease may experience accumulation of metronidazole metabolites, necessitating monitoring for toxicity. 4. Fungal Superinfections: Overgrowth of Candida may occur during therapy, requiring antifungal treatment. 5. Blood Dyscrasias: Use with caution in patients with a history of blood dyscrasias. Leukopenia has been observed but is typically reversible. Drug Interactions: Alcohol: Disulfiram-like reactions may occur. Warfarin: Potentiation of anticoagulant effects, requiring monitoring of prothrombin time and INR. Lithium: Elevated serum lithium levels and potential toxicity. Busulfan: Increased plasma concentrations and risk of toxicity. CYP450 Enzyme Modulators: Drugs like cimetidine may prolong metronidazole’s half-life, while inducers like phenytoin may accelerate its elimination. Use in Specific Populations: Pregnancy: Category B. While no definitive teratogenic effects have been observed, metronidazole crosses the placenta, and its effects on fetal organogenesis are unknown. Nursing Mothers: Metronidazole is present in breast milk at concentrations similar to maternal serum levels. Due to potential tumorigenicity, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug. Patient Counseling: Patients should be informed that metronidazole is only effective against bacterial and parasitic infections and should not be used for viral infections. Adherence to the prescribed regimen is crucial to prevent treatment failure and the development of drug resistance. Alcohol consumption should be avoided during and for at least three days after therapy. Patients should report any neurological symptoms or adverse effects to their physician immediately.
